abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent psychostimulant that primarily acts on the dopaminergic system and has strong reinforcing effects. It also induces oxidative stress, impairs mitochondrial function, and causes neurotoxicity at high doses. We previously showed that long-term METH self-administration increases mitochondrial respiratory metabolism and reduces antioxidant capacity in the mesolimbic dopaminergic circuit. However, the effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure in dopamine neurons remained unexplored. Here, we examine the acute effects of METH on mitochondrial morphology using a methodology that combines classical immunofluorescence labeling with advanced computational clearing methods and quantitative morphometric analysis. We administered acute METH treatments to mice at doses known to produce stimulant (3 mg/kg) or neurotoxic (20 mg/kg) effects. One week later, quantitative morphological analysis showed that neurotoxic METH exposure increased mitochondrial fragmentation in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons, significantly reducing mitochondrial size and length while increasing estimated roundness. By contrast, NeuN-labeled non-dopaminergic VTA neurons showed no changes in mitochondrial morphology, suggesting that acute susceptibility to METH-induced mitochondrial fragmentation is cell-type-specific in dopamine neurons. In addition, dopamine neuron size decreased, particularly after the neurotoxic METH dose. Our findings shed light on the lasting effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure and can help explain the early mechanisms underlying mitochondrial functional changes in VTA dopamine neurons.
